CASE TITLE:
Production ML Value Realization

CASE:
A predictive maintenance ML solution at a manufacturing firm performed exceptionally well during a 3-month proof-of-concept testing phase (92% accuracy). However, six months after deployment into production, the business sponsor reports it is struggling to deliver the expected financial value, and maintenance costs remain unchanged.

INSTRUCTIONS:
Diagnose the likely causes for the discrepancy between testing performance and production value. Outline your methodology for investigating the issue and recommend an enterprise approach to remediate it.

CANDIDATE RESPONSE:
Diagnosis: Why 92% Accuracy Didn't Translate to Value

1. Accuracy ≠ business impact
92% model accuracy is a technical metric, not a financial one. It says nothing about precision/recall trade-offs on rare failure events, false positive costs (unnecessary maintenance triggered), or false negative costs (missed failures still causing downtime). A model can be "accurate" overall while missing the specific high-cost failure modes that actually drive maintenance spend.

2. Data drift between POC and production
The 3-month POC likely used a curated, stable dataset from a specific set of machines/conditions. Production introduces new equipment, sensor degradation, seasonal effects, or operating condition changes the model never saw — silently eroding real-world performance even if it "looks" fine on paper.

3. Workflow/adoption gap
A prediction is not an outcome. If maintenance teams aren't acting on alerts (due to alert fatigue, distrust, unclear ownership, or the alerts not fitting into existing scheduling/ERP workflows), the model can be technically correct and still change nothing operationally.

4. Wrong or diluted KPI linkage
"Maintenance costs unchanged" could mean the model is preventing failures, but savings are being offset elsewhere (e.g., increased preventive maintenance labor, parts ordered too early, no reduction in headcount/schedules despite fewer breakdowns). The financial benefit may exist but isn't being measured or captured operationally.

5. Base rate / scope mismatch
If catastrophic failures were already rare, even a good model has limited dollars to save — the POC's accuracy number may have been measured against a dataset with more balanced fail/no-fail examples than the true production distribution.

text:
Translating Diagnosis into a Commercial Recommendation

Step 1: Convert findings into a "so what"
Each diagnostic finding needs to answer: what specific lever does this point to, and what's the size of the prize? E.g., "Volume decline concentrated in Region X due to a competitor's price cut" → the lever is competitive repricing or value-add differentiation in that region, sized at $Y of the $12%.

Step 2: Build a menu of options against each root cause
For each diagnosed driver (price, volume, mix, external/internal), generate 2–3 candidate interventions — e.g., for volume loss: targeted promotions, channel expansion, win-back campaigns; for mix shift: upsell/cross-sell programs, portfolio rationalization.

Step 3: Prioritize using a structured framework

Impact vs. Effort (2x2) matrix — quick filter to separate "quick wins" from "major bets" and deprioritize low-impact/high-effort options.
Cost-benefit / NPV analysis — quantify expected revenue recovery vs. implementation cost and time-to-value for shortlisted options; this converts diagnosis into a business case leadership can act on.
Strategic fit screen — assess each option against the company's stated strategy, brand positioning, and capabilities (an option might recover revenue but conflict with a premium positioning, for instance — that's a real trade-off to surface, not ignore).
Portfolio/sequencing view — not all fixes happen at once; sequence based on urgency (stop the bleeding) vs. sustainable fixes (structural repositioning, pricing architecture overhaul).

CASE TITLE:
GenAI Customer Operations Transformation

CASE:

The board is pushing for AI adoption, but the operations team is concerned about risks, hallucination, and job displacement.

INSTRUCTIONS:
Please provide a structured assessment of this situation. Discuss the business value, potential risks, transformation implications, operating considerations, and a recommended implementation approach.

RISKS: Key risks include model hallucinations, data privacy violations, CRM integration bottlenecks, and employee displacement anxiety. 3. TRANSFORMATION IMPLICATIONS: Requires a robust change management strategy positioning GenAI as an agent copilot rather than replacement, plus targeted upskilling. 4. OPERATING CONSIDERATIONS: Establish human-in-the-loop guardrails, CRM middleware APIs, real-time safety auditing, and clear escalation paths. 5. RECOMMENDED APPROACH: Phase 1: Deploy agent-assist tools internally to build trust. Phase 2: Pilot customer-facing self-service for low-risk intents. Phase 3: Full end-to-end automated workflows with CRM synchronization.
